newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish govt wins confidence vote over legal blunder.
newsitem.headline: Irish govt wins confidence vote over legal blunder.

text.p: The Irish government comfortably survived a vote of confidence on Wednesday night over a legal blunder which led to the brief release of 16 top security prisoners including IRA guerrilla suspects.
Prime Minister John Bruton's left-right coalition won the vote 79-70 after a two-day debate dominated by opposition calls that Justice Minister Nora Owen resign over the debacle.

It was the first vote of confidence in Bruton's so-called Rainbow Coalition since it came to power two years ago this month after former Prime Minister Albert Reynolds' government collapsed in a row over legal appointments.

Bruton's coalition of his own Fine Gael party, Deputy Prime Minister Dick Spring's Labour party and the small Democratic Left grouping came through the confidence vote unscathed in what were seen as the opening shots in campaigns for a general election which must be held by November next year.
The coalition has a five-seat majority in the 116-member house. Many parliamentarians were not present for the vote or had been paired.

"We will remain united and solid together, working on a basis of trust," Spring told critics on the opposition Fianna Fail benches who are already making law and order a major plank in their general election campaigning.

The vote was called after 16 top-security prisoners, including Nessan Quinlivan, whose extradition is sought by Britain beause of his alleged IRA links, were released from custody last week because of a major mix-up over the legality of a Special Criminal Court.

One of their lawyers complained that the judge of the court, Dominic Lynch, had asked to be removed from his duties and that the cabinet had agreed to his request to step down in August. The prisoners were set free and immediately re-arrested.
But Lynch had not been told of the cabinet's agreement, leading to charges that the court was unconstitutional and that the judge had no power.

Bruton told parliament on Tuesday that the administration of the courts and prison service were being taken out of the Justice Ministry's workload under proposals dating back for some time but the opposition said Owen was being punished by having half her responsibilities removed.

Spring argued that the coalition was working for a more efficient government and had carried out similar streamlining in the Finance and Comunications ministry by setting up special bodies to deal with government debt and the overhaul of the telephone network.
